extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students of science, and informed citizens interested in scientific method and the application of science to social problems
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for conducting and evaluating scientific inquiry: how to collect and classify facts, infer relationships and laws, apply disciplined imagination, avoid dogma, and use scientific results responsibly in social judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific method: classification then relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific method consists in the orderly classification of facts followed by the recognition of their relationship and recurring sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises starting with accurate classification of facts, then tracing correlations and sequences; this procedural order distinguishes scientific inquiry from speculative approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific judgment: impartial and evidence-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific judgment is the judgment based upon this recognition and free from personal bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to practical unanimity among investigators approaching the same facts; anti-patterns include judgments based on personal prejudice or untested intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate classification of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate and laborious classification of facts is essential before drawing conclusions; inadequate classification produces ignorance or error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: alchemy required reclassification to become chemistry; poor classification underlies astrology and witchcraft. Scoring note: work is weak if classifications are sloppy or premature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of relationships and recurring sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: After classifying facts, science must recognise relationships and recurring sequences among them to form generalisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognition is the basis for formulating laws and predictions; failure to identify genuine recurring patterns leads to spurious theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplined imagination in discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative imagination is necessary to discover single statements or brief formulae (laws) that summarise wide ranges of facts, but this imagination must be disciplined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The imagination must appreciate the full range of facts and be followed by severe testing; anti-pattern: unrestrained imagination that 'solves the universe' without testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing and severe criticism of hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proposed law or imaginative hypothesis must be tested and criticised in every conceivable way until certain that it agrees with the whole group of phenomena it purports to summarise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faraday's remark: many thoughts are crushed by the investigator's own severe criticism; the essence of scientific use of imagination is rigorous criticism and testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest confession of ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Science must frankly admit ignorance where classification and knowledge are insufficient, rather than prematurely constructing systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting 'I am ignorant' is healthy; constructing dogmatic systems on unsettled facts is an anti-pattern. Patience and further classification are required before conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of dogma and system-mongering
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical or theological dogmas and system-mongering are dangerous when they constrain scientific research or claim exclusive authority over problems science can address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: theological suppression of heliocentrism; anti-patterns include declaring fields 'not the legitimate problems of science' and thereby blocking inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exclude fields a priori from scientific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever there is the slightest possibility for the human mind to know, it is a legitimate problem of science; science should not fence off unexplored fields as beyond its method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against pronouncing certain classes of facts inherently unreachable by scientific method; instead investigate classification and method applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish unreal/self-contradictory facts from genuine phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Some putative facts are unreal or self-contradictory (e.g., astrology, witchcraft, certain Spiritualist claims) and cannot be described scientifically; these should be identified and set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If facts are internally inconsistent they cannot be reduced to law; but where real phenomena exist (e.g., hypnotic conditions) apply classification and method to understand them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term patient toil for difficult problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Many problems (e.g., psychical or biological enigmas) may require centuries of careful classification and collective work before definite scientific judgments can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Atlantic cable required long foundations before practicability; scoring: unrealistic claims of near-term solution reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal validity as touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: The touchstone of science is the universal validity of its results for all normally constituted and duly instructed minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a system's conclusions do not hold universally under informed scrutiny, they are likely metaphysical imagination rather than scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific training as civic requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Training in scientific methods—appreciation of evidence, classification of facts, elimination of personal bias—is essential for good citizenship and formation of moral/social judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or social judgments depend first on knowledge and method; example: responsible voting based on informed judgment is superior civic action to vague philanthropy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply scientific results to social policy cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific theories (e.g., heredity) can and should influence social and moral policy, but conclusions may be tentative and open to modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scientific classification and correlation to inform policy (e.g., welfare, education), but avoid dogmatic application of unsettled theories; consider alternatives and uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure science has unpredictable practical value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations and laws discovered by pure science, even if seeming theoretical, often become the basis for far-reaching technical applications (e.g., Galvani -> telegraph, Hertz -> wireless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification for endowment of pure science: do not evaluate research solely by immediate utility. Anti-pattern: denying support for pure research because short-term application is not obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science combines imagination with severe self-criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific use of imagination is creative but must be accompanied by the investigator's severe criticism and adverse examination of preliminary conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many promising ideas are rightly discarded by their originators through self-critique; a good scientist fosters imaginative hypotheses and equally rigorous self-testing.
